flashcards.q: What exactly is the risk of never restoring a backup to test it?
flashcards.a: On the day of a disaster you may find the file empty, corrupt or useless without its key. A "successful" job doesn't tell you the backup can be restored.
flashcards.more: A successful job only means the command finished. A full disk, a wrong directory or a lost key can make the file useless. Only restoring it and checking the data gives proof.

flashcards.q: What are RPO and RTO?
flashcards.a: RPO: the most data, in time, you can tolerate losing. RTO: how quickly you must be running again.
flashcards.more: An RPO of 1 minute means you must save almost all data (so you need PITR). An RTO of 1 hour means the restore must finish within an hour. The business sets these two numbers, and then the backup design has to meet them.

flashcards.q: What is the 3-2-1 rule for backups?
flashcards.a: Keep 3 copies of the data, on 2 kinds of storage, with 1 of them at another location (offsite).
flashcards.more: Three copies in the same safe are really one copy: fire, flood or an attacker takes them all together. A separate location plus immutability (no deletes) also protects you from ransomware.

flashcards.q: Is a replica a substitute for a backup?
flashcards.a: No. A replica copies every change instantly, including a mistaken DELETE and ransomware.
flashcards.more: A replica is for staying up (availability), not for going back to an earlier moment. To go back in time, you need backups and WAL.

flashcards.q: How does point-in-time recovery (PITR) work?
flashcards.a: You restore a base backup, then replay the archived WAL logs and stop at the chosen moment, for example 1 minute before the mistake.
flashcards.more: The nightly backup is just one picture; the WAL stores every transaction in between. Together they let you reach any moment. A small `archive_timeout` brings the RPO down to seconds or minutes.

flashcards.q: Why is a PITR restore done on a new or scratch server?
flashcards.a: Restoring over the live DB wipes all current data. On a separate server you can verify first and bring back only the data you need.
flashcards.more: Valid transactions made after the mistake exist too. Roll the whole DB back and you lose them. So you first recover elsewhere, extract the deleted data, and then put it into production.

flashcards.q: How do you put recovered rows back without losing newer valid data?
flashcards.a: Load them into a staging table on production, then `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Rows that exist today stay; only the lost ones come in.
flashcards.more: Orders placed since the mistake exist only in production, and restoring over them would destroy them. The staging table lets the database decide row by row, using the primary key.

flashcards.q: What is a restore drill, and how often should you run one?
flashcards.a: Loading the latest backup into a scratch DB, timing it and verifying the data. At least weekly, automatically.
flashcards.more: The time measured in the drill is your real RTO. As data grows, restores slow down and the RTO quietly rises. Measuring regularly catches that.

flashcards.q: What is a runbook, and what makes a good one?
flashcards.a: Written instructions to follow in an emergency: short ordered steps, copy-paste commands, expected results, when to stop, and an owner.
flashcards.more: Nobody can build a plan at 3 a.m.; they can follow one. If a runbook isn't updated after every drill or incident, within a few months it is wrong.

flashcards.q: Which four safeguards should be in place before a bulk replay?
flashcards.a: An idempotent handler, a throttle (a speed limit), a dry run and a checkpoint.
flashcards.more: You need all four together. Miss one and you risk double processing, overloading your own system, running the wrong thing, or starting over when you stop partway.

flashcards.q: Why can a replay itself become a second incident?
flashcards.a: Pouring every failed job in at once hits the system hard, and jobs that were partly done run twice.
flashcards.more: 4000 failed jobs arriving at once is extra load on top of normal traffic, with gateway 429s and exhausted DB connections. Recovery too has to be planned, slow and safe.

flashcards.q: What is a dry run, and what is it for?
flashcards.a: It only counts how many jobs would run, without running anything. A wrong filter or assumption is caught early.
flashcards.more: With `--dry-run` the command doesn't dispatch and doesn't save a checkpoint. You look at the output (how many, what limits, a few samples) and only then do the real run.

flashcards.q: What does a checkpoint do in a replay?
flashcards.a: It saves the last processed id, so after a stop or crash the run resumes from there.
flashcards.more: Without a checkpoint you restart from the beginning after a crash, and work already done runs again. After each batch, an upsert goes into the `replay_checkpoint` table.

flashcards.q: How is speed limited in a replay?
flashcards.a: A pause after every dispatch (20 per second), and few workers on a separate transport for replay.
flashcards.more: The aim is to run the recovery without slowing normal work. You raise the speed gradually while watching CPU, DB connections and error rate on the dashboard.

flashcards.q: Why fetch batches with `id > :after` instead of OFFSET?
flashcards.a: With a large OFFSET, every earlier row must be skipped each time, which is slow. `id > :after` jumps straight there through the index.
flashcards.more: This is called keyset pagination. The last id is our checkpoint too, so one thing does both jobs.

flashcards.q: How does a replay avoid both a second email and a missing one?
flashcards.a: It never emails directly. It queues one receipt row per event (UNIQUE event_id), and a separate sender emails each unsent row once.
flashcards.more: A sent email can't be recalled, so doubles must not happen. A plain "skip emails in a replay" switch would also skip receipts the first attempt missed. A unique row per event covers both.

flashcards.q: The first attempt credited a customer but failed before the receipt. What does the replay do?
flashcards.a: The processed_event guard skips the credit, but the receipt row is still inserted, and the sender emails it once.
flashcards.more: The credit and the receipt have separate guards, so each is decided on its own. The sender sends only rows with no `sent_at`, a few at a time, so even a backlog of 600 drains calmly.

flashcards.q: What is the simple way to make a handler idempotent?
flashcards.a: Keep a UNIQUE `processed_event(event_id)`, INSERT in the same transaction as the work, and if 0 rows were inserted, skip the work.
flashcards.more: With the INSERT and the real write in one transaction, after a crash either both exist or neither does. So running again does the work exactly once.

flashcards.q: Why is running a direct UPDATE from the console in production risky?
flashcards.a: It leaves no evidence, loses the old values, and if the condition is too broad, changes the right rows along with the wrong ones.
flashcards.more: A condition written in a hurry is often too wide. With no before and after values recorded, spotting the mistake, reversing it, or explaining it to an auditor all become hard.

flashcards.q: What is a corrective entry?
flashcards.a: A new, documented record of a correction, written instead of erasing the mistake; the original error stays in the history too.
flashcards.more: In a ledger it is a reversing entry followed by a new entry with the correct amount. That keeps debit = credit intact and lets an auditor see the whole story.

flashcards.q: How do you fix a money mistake in a ledger, and what do you never do?
flashcards.a: You do: a reversing entry plus a new correct entry. You never do: UPDATE or DELETE an old entry.
flashcards.more: A data-fix script doesn't change money entries in the ledger. Every money correction goes through the posting service as a transaction. For example, a deposit posted as $5,000 instead of $500: the $5,000 stays, a reversal of $5,000 is added, then a correct deposit of $500. The net is $500, and debit = credit still holds.

flashcards.q: Why does an audited data-fix script have an "expected count"?
flashcards.a: If the counted number of rows doesn't match the expected one, the script changes nothing. A wrong condition is caught before it runs.
flashcards.more: In review everyone agrees "2300 rows will change." If 14,300 turn up at run time, the condition is too broad, so it stops.

flashcards.q: Why does a data-fix script write the UPDATE and the log in one statement?
flashcards.a: So that a change always comes with a log entry, and a change without one can't happen. The before and after values also let you reverse the fix.
flashcards.more: In PostgreSQL, `WITH fixed AS (UPDATE ... RETURNING ...) INSERT INTO data_fix_log SELECT ...` is a single statement, so it all runs in one transaction.

flashcards.q: How do you undo a data-fix script that turned out to be wrong?
flashcards.a: Update the rows back from `data_fix_log`, but only those still in the state the fix left (`status = new_value`).
flashcards.more: The log holds each row's old and new value. The `new_value` guard means a row that someone changed after the fix isn't overwritten with an old value.

flashcards.q: What should happen if you run a data-fix script again?
flashcards.a: Nothing. The condition no longer matches the fixed rows, so 0 rows change.
flashcards.more: So running it twice by mistake, or again after a crash, doesn't cause a double fix. That is an idempotent fix, safe to run again.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between roll back and roll forward?
flashcards.a: Roll back returns to the earlier version. Roll forward deploys a small fix and moves ahead.
flashcards.more: Rolling back is fast when only the code changed. If data or schema has changed (a column was dropped, say), going backwards is dangerous, so you roll forward.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't rolling back the code fix bad data?
flashcards.a: A roll back restores only the code. The data the bad code already wrote stays in the database.
flashcards.more: So fixing the deploy and correcting the data are two separate jobs. Do the second with an audited script and corrective entries, so that later you can understand what happened.
